title: A Blameless Culture Starts in the First Minute of the Postmortem
summary: Blameless doesn't mean nobody's accountable. How to run incident reviews that ask how instead of who, write action items that fix systems and keep people honest.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Tuesday, 10 a.m., the morning after a 40-minute outage. The postmortem doc is up on the big screen. Everyone in the room knows which deploy caused it, and everyone knows whose name is on that deploy. The doc's title says "learning review". For the first minute, though, nobody talks. The room is waiting to find out whether one person is about to carry the whole story alone.

That minute is where a blameless culture gets decided. "We don't blame people" is easy to say on a good week. It gets hard when customers were hit, a VP wants a timeline and someone in the incident channel has already typed "who pushed this?". This post covers what blameless actually means, how to run the review so the real story comes out, and the small things leads do that make the next incident report more honest, or less.

Blameless doesn't mean nobody's accountable

Google's SRE book gives the working definition. A blameless postmortem focuses on "identifying the contributing causes of the incident without indicting any individual or team." It also spells out the assumption underneath: "everyone involved in an incident had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had" (Site Reliability Engineering, Postmortem Culture).

That assumption trips people up, because it sounds like nobody is responsible. It works the other way round. Blameless separates accountability from punishment. Accountability means explaining what happened, what you saw, what you assumed and what should change, then owning the follow-up. Punishment asks for a name, fast enough that everyone can feel the matter is closed. Only one of those produces fixes.

The cost of getting it wrong is spelled out in the same chapter: in a blame culture, people stop bringing issues to light for fear of punishment. DORA's research connects this to delivery. It uses Ron Westrum's typology, which sorts organizations by how they handle information and failure:

Westrum culture type When something fails People who bring bad news are
Pathological (power-oriented) Scapegoating Punished
Bureaucratic (rule-oriented) "Justice" Neglected
Generative (performance-oriented) Inquiry Trained

DORA reports that a high-trust, generative culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance (DORA, Generative organizational culture). Blameless reviews are one of the most concrete ways to move a team toward that bottom row.

The person at the end of the chain

Most outages aren't one dramatic mistake. They're a chain of small gaps that each looked fine on their own. A dashboard that didn't show the metric that mattered. A rollback path nobody had tested. A deploy checklist people tick from memory. An alert that had fired falsely for months, so everyone learned to ignore it. A review that checked style but not failure modes. A new teammate who learned the release process by watching someone else do it once. The person who pressed the last button is the most visible link. The chain was there long before they showed up.

Hindsight makes it worse. Once you know the outcome, every step toward it looks obviously wrong. It didn't look that way at the time, or nobody would have taken it.

Swap "why" for "how" and "what"

John Allspaw, who ran operations at Etsy, makes the case in The Infinite Hows. Asking "why?" too easily gets you to an answer to "who?". Asking "how?" gets you to describe the conditions that let the event happen. He borrows questions from Gary Klein and Sidney Dekker, such as "What were you seeing?", "What were you expecting to happen?" and "Did you ask anyone for help?" The aim is to learn how it made sense for someone to do what they did.

Instead of Try
"Why did you deploy on a Friday afternoon?" "What did the release calendar and the checklist tell you at that point?"
"Why didn't you know about the migration?" "Where was that knowledge supposed to live, and how would someone new find it?"
"Why did you ignore the alert?" "How often had that alert fired falsely in the last month?"
"Who approved this?" "What did the reviewer see in the diff, and what wasn't in it?"

Nothing in the right column lets the problem off the hook. Every answer points at something the team can actually change.

Write it down so the system learns

A blameless review needs a document to match. The timeline should record what people observed, what they decided, what context they had and what nobody knew yet. Then come the action items, and here Google's SRE workbook is blunt. Words like "Improve" and "Make better" are "vague and open to interpretation." Each item needs an owner, a tracking ticket, a priority and an end state you can verify. The workbook also notes that "trying to change human behavior is less reliable than changing automated systems and processes" (The Site Reliability Workbook, Postmortem Culture).

  • Weak: "Be more careful with migrations." Better: "Add a pre-deploy check that blocks a migration without a tested rollback script. Owner: platform team, with a ticket."
  • Weak: "Remind people not to run the cleanup job twice." Better: "Make the cleanup job safe to run twice." The workbook's own good example is close to this: commands should be idempotent, or at least fail safe when repeated.
  • Weak: "Improve alerting." Better: "Tune the payment-service alert until false alarms are rare enough that on-call trusts it, then review the threshold after a month."

Then follow up. The workbook quotes Ben Treynor Sloss: "a postmortem without subsequent action is indistinguishable from no postmortem." Keep open action items on a regular review agenda until they're done.

What leads do in the first five minutes

Leads shape this mostly through small reactions. If the first person who tells the full story gets a cold reply in the channel, or a mark in their next performance review, the next incident report will contain less truth. People will report later, smooth the timeline and leave out what they weren't sure about. A team can't fix a system it's afraid to describe.

A few things that help:

  • Open the review by stating the goal out loud: understand how this happened and what to change. Nobody is on trial.
  • Thank the person who raised the alarm or wrote the first honest update, by name, in public.
  • When someone asks "who did this?", redirect without drama: "Let's get the timeline straight first, then the causes."
  • Reward good postmortems. The SRE book describes a monthly "postmortem of the month" shared with the whole organization, and says writing effective postmortems should be rewarded and celebrated.

Individual growth still has a place. Someone may need pairing, more context on a risky part of the system or closer review for a while. Handle that in a 1:1, away from the incident review. People can make fewer mistakes with effort, sure. The bigger question is whether your system still supports good decisions when people are tired, rushed, new or missing context.

Blameless starts before anything breaks

The best sign a team is getting this right shows up on ordinary days. A developer reports a near miss before it turns into an outage. QA says "I'm not confident about this one" instead of signing off anyway. Support mentions a pattern in tickets before the dashboards catch it. All of that depends on people believing that honesty leads to fixes and not to embarrassment. There's more on raising problems early in Why Good Teams Surface Risk Early.

Old habits come back under pressure. Someone will still ask who caused it. Someone will still want a one-line answer for leadership. Keep the rhythm anyway: slow down, rebuild the context, protect the people who told the truth, pick concrete fixes and check later that they shipped.

Try this week

  • Put the SRE book's assumption at the top of your postmortem template: everyone did the right thing with the information they had.
  • In your next review, swap one "why" for "what were you seeing at that point?"
  • Rewrite one vague action item ("be more careful") as a system change with an owner and a ticket.
  • Open your last three postmortems and count how many action items actually shipped.

faqs.a: Google's SRE book defines it as a postmortem that identifies the contributing causes of an incident without indicting any individual or team. It assumes everyone involved had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had, then looks for system changes that make the next good decision easier.

faqs.q: Does blameless mean nobody is held accountable?
faqs.a: No. Blameless separates accountability from punishment. People still explain what happened, what they saw and assumed, and they own the follow-up actions. What goes away is naming someone quickly so the incident feels closed, which tends to make people hide problems next time.

faqs.q: What questions should we ask in an incident review?
faqs.a: Prefer how and what over why and who. John Allspaw suggests questions such as "What were you seeing?", "What were you expecting to happen?" and "Did you ask anyone for help?". They rebuild the context someone had, so the team can see how a decision made sense at the time.

faqs.q: What makes a good postmortem action item?
faqs.a: Google's SRE workbook asks for an owner, a tracking ticket, a priority and an end state you can verify. Avoid vague verbs like "improve". Prefer changes to systems and automation over asking people to be more careful, because changing human behavior is less reliable.

faqs.q: How can leaders build a blameless culture?
faqs.a: State the goal at the start of every review, thank people who raise problems early, redirect "who did this?" toward the timeline, reward well-written postmortems and handle any individual coaching privately in a 1:1. Check that action items actually ship.
